prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "GOLD FIELDS LTD" (ticker GFI). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Gold Fields fails most Rule Breaker traits: it is a mid-sized producer in a mature commodity industry with no brand or product edge, and its shares fell about 15% over the past year. It does have good recent execution and a strong balance sheet, but Gardner looks for top dogs in emerging industries, which this is not.
summaries.buffett: Buffett generally avoids commodity producers whose earnings depend on a price they cannot set; Gold Fields' profit attributable jumped from $703.3M in 2023 to $3,567.4M in 2025 largely because of the gold price. Its balance sheet is now strong (net debt $437M at June 2026), but there is no durable moat and its key assets depend on government leases such as Tarkwa's, which expire in April 2027.
summaries.munger: Munger would note the business is easy to understand but is a price taker with no pricing power, and inverting shows several ways to lose: a gold-price fall, losing the Tarkwa lease as it lost Damang in 2025, or overpaying in large deals like the rejected A$38.7bn Northern Star bid. The low P/E of about 7.5 reflects those risks more than a bargain on a wonderful business.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify Gold Fields as a cyclical whose earnings follow the gold price; the classic cyclical trap is buying at a low P/E (about 7.5 now) near peak prices. Revenue grew every year from 2020 to 2025 and the dividend yield is about 5%, but the story depends on gold staying high and on Ghana renewing Tarkwa.
summaries.fisher: Fisher's growth-company points fit poorly: there is no product R&D or sales organisation to speak of, and growth comes from developing new mines (Salares Norte, Windfall) and acquisitions. Management under Mike Fraser has delivered on operations, but long-term above-average growth in sales and margins is not under its control.
summaries.graham: On Graham's defensive criteria Gold Fields is large and has paid dividends every year since at least 1999, but it had losses within the last ten years, and its P/E times P/B (about 7.5 x 3.6 = 27) exceeds 22.5. The price is cheap against peak earnings rather than against average earnings over several years.
summaries.thiel: Thiel's monopoly test fails: Gold Fields sells an undifferentiated commodity into a perfectly competitive market, with no proprietary technology or network effects. Its only unique edges are specific ore bodies, which are finite.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner's focus on durable growth, efficiency and rational capital allocation gives a mixed picture: Gold Fields is very cash-generative (2025 adjusted free cash flow $2.97bn) and returned $1.7bn for 2025, but growth depends on gold prices and large M&A, and it is not tied to tech platform shifts like AI.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller-style macro investing could favour gold miners when real rates fall and central banks buy gold, but gold has faded from early-2026 records to about $4,200/oz and Gold Fields' shares are down about 15% in a year with deal and Ghana overhangs. Earnings momentum is still positive (consensus FY2026 revenue about $11.9bn vs $8.75bn), so the case rests on the gold-price view.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical, capital-intensive commodity businesses with no pricing power; Gold Fields' recent high returns come from the gold price rather than from a consistently high return on capital. It does not fit the 'buy good companies' leg of his approach.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Gold Fields currently screens well: EV/EBIT is about 5.6 and trailing return on capital is about 40%, both driven by record gold prices. Greenblatt's method would include it mechanically, though these figures are cyclical peaks rather than normal levels.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool (great business, talented and honest managers, ability to reinvest at high rates) is only partly met: management is competent and capital returns are disciplined, but mining is not an inherently great business and reinvestment returns on new mines like Windfall (capex up to $1.9bn) are uncertain.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks simple businesses in temporary distress with low downside; Gold Fields is simple and has a temporary setback (Tarkwa lease, rejected bid, share price down from $61.64 to about $36), but the Tarkwa risk is a real permanent-loss risk and the low P/E reflects high gold prices.
summaries.wood: Gold Fields has no exposure to ARK's disruptive platforms (AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain, multiomics); it is a traditional gold miner whose market will not grow many times over. It does not fit Wood's framework.
summaries.ackman: Ackman seeks simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and pricing power; Gold Fields is simple and currently generates lots of free cash, but its cash flows are unpredictable and it has no pricing power or barriers beyond its mineral rights.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model does not apply: Gold Fields cannot pass scale savings to customers in a commodity market, and its long-term position depends on depleting ore bodies and host governments rather than a compounding customer advantage.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing markets solving large problems with technology; gold mining is a slow-growing, mature market and Gold Fields is not a technology company. It fits his criteria poorly.

momentum.evidence: GFI fell about 15% over the 52 weeks to October 2026 (to $36.34 from a 52-week high of $61.64), lagging the S&P 500 and peers such as AngloGold Ashanti, after the rejected Northern Star bid and Tarkwa lease uncertainty.

g4.evidence: CEO Mike Fraser (ex-BHP, South32) has delivered strong 2025 results, and the stock is about 96% owned by institutions, but no famous investor or strategic partner is known to back it.

g6.evidence: Commentators generally call it cheap (P/E about 7.5, consensus price target about $49.5 vs $36.34), not overvalued.

simple.evidence: It digs gold (96% of 2025 revenue) from nine mines and sells it at the spot price, a business a generalist can understand, though the gold price is hard to forecast.

b2.evidence: Results swing with the gold price: profit attributable was $703.3M in 2023, $1,245.0M in 2024 and $3,567.4M in 2025, and it reported losses in the late 2010s.

integrity.evidence: It is JSE/NYSE-listed with PwC as auditor, pays out 35% of pre-discretionary free cash flow as base dividends and openly flagged the Tarkwa risk, but the large Northern Star bid at a low premium raised questions about capital allocation.

b6.evidence: Gold Fields followed the industry consolidation trend with the A$3.7bn Gold Road deal and a A$38.7bn approach for Northern Star, which some see as size-seeking, though it is also returning $1.25bn in extra dividends and buybacks.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 42% on trailing figures with low debt, but that reflects record gold prices; returns were far lower in 2023 (profit $703.3M on revenue $4,500.7M) and in loss years of the late 2010s.

fcf.evidence: In 2025 net cash from operations of $4,534.1M less PP&E additions of $1,398.5M left $3,135.6M, about 88% of profit attributable, and H1 2026 adjusted free cash flow was $2,225.3M.

b10.evidence: Retained cash built Salares Norte and bought Gold Road, lifting output 18% in 2025, but past spending (e.g. South Deep) produced write-downs, and much of the value gain came from gold prices.

safety.evidence: At $36.34 the stock trades at about 7.5x trailing earnings and a 13% free-cash-flow yield, but at a gold price that may not last and with the Tarkwa lease (about 16% of output) at risk, so the margin of safety is uncertain.

fairprice.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 7.5, forward P/E about 7.8 and dividend yield about 5% are reasonable for a mid-cycle-quality gold miner.

mu5.evidence: It could be hurt by a gold-price drop, losing mining leases (Damang 2025, Tarkwa expiring April 2027), cost overruns at Windfall, mine accidents or an overpriced takeover.

reinvest.evidence: It plans about $2bn a year of capital spending and targets 2.8-3.1Moz by 2031, but returns on new mines like Windfall (capex up to $1.9bn, permit delays) depend on gold prices.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear cyclical: earnings track the gold price, and the story is higher output from Salares Norte, Gruyere and Windfall while gold stays high.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E about 7.5 is far below recent EPS growth (diluted EPS $1.38 in 2024 to $3.94 in 2025), though Lynch warns low P/Es in cyclicals can signal a peak.

runway.evidence: Production can grow from 2.44Moz (2025) toward 2.8-3.1Moz by 2031 via Windfall and acquisitions, but gold mining is mature and each mine depletes.

ly7.evidence: The company completed buybacks (shares in issue net of treasury 890.9M at June 2026 vs about 895.0M in issue), but there is no evidence of notable insider buying, and insider ownership is about 0.03%.

ly8.evidence: Gold mining is a 'boring' niche and Gold Fields is less followed than Newmont, but it is covered by about 11 analysts and is held about 96% by institutions.

fi2.evidence: As mines mature it develops new ones (Salares Norte, Windfall) and buys others (Gold Road), the mining equivalent of new products.

fi3.evidence: Exploration spending ($297.8M expensed in 2025) has found and extended ore bodies such as Windfall and Salares Norte, but results are uneven.

fi4.evidence: It has no meaningful sales effort; gold is sold to refiners and banks at the spot price.

longterm.evidence: Management invests in decade-long projects (Windfall first gold 2029, life-extension plans) while also paying out about 54% of 2025 adjusted free cash flow to shareholders.

gr1.evidence: It is a large company with a market value of about $33bn and 2025 revenue of $8,751.3M.

ni10.evidence: Gold Fields reported net losses attributable in the late 2010s (including 2018, after large impairments at South Deep), so it was not profitable in each of the last ten years.

gr4.evidence: Dividend records show at least one dividend paid every calendar year from 1999 through 2026.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS reached $3.94 in 2025 versus losses or small profits a decade earlier, far more than one-third growth.

gr6.evidence: Against 2023-2025 average diluted EPS of about $2.03, the $36.34 price is about 18 times average earnings, above Graham's 15.

gr7.evidence: P/E about 7.5 times P/B about 3.6 is roughly 27, above Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: It has no proprietary technology; its gold is identical to competitors'.

timing.evidence: Gold above $4,000/oz makes this a very profitable time for miners, but prices have faded from early-2026 records.

th3.evidence: It holds about 2% of global gold mine output, a small share of a large, mature market.

team.evidence: Mike Fraser (CEO since 2024, ex-BHP and South32) is an experienced professional manager, not an exceptional founder.

th5.evidence: Distribution is not a problem: refiners and bullion banks buy all of its gold at the market price.

durable.evidence: Gold demand is likely to last for decades, but individual mines deplete and leases can be lost, so its position depends on replacing its 48.3Moz of reserves.

th7.evidence: Its opportunities (Australian consolidation, Canadian development) are pursued by many rivals, such as Northern Star, Newmont and Agnico Eagle.

trend.evidence: It benefits from central-bank and investor gold buying, but not from technology platform shifts like AI or cloud.

dr1.evidence: H1 2026 profit attributable rose to $1,854.6M from $1,026.7M, but headline EPS of 208 US cents missed expectations of about 270 cents and gold has eased from its peak.

dr2.evidence: It depends on the Tarkwa lease outcome by April 2027, the Windfall permit and whether a Northern Star deal is revived, none of which is predictable.

dr4.evidence: Lower real interest rates and central-bank gold buying support gold, but the gold price has softened from early-2026 highs to about $4,200/oz.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include a Tarkwa lease renewal, Windfall environmental approval expected around end-2026, the $1.25bn extra shareholder returns and possible renewed Northern Star talks.

dr7.evidence: Binary risks (Tarkwa lease, large M&A) and gold-price dependence make it hard to justify a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin (revenue less cost of sales) reached 57.9% in 2025, but this comes from high gold prices rather than pricing power and was 39.0% in 2023.

fcfyield.evidence: Free-cash-flow yield is about 13% on trailing figures, attractive for a business with modest long-term growth.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 5.6 (enterprise value about $34bn), meaning operating profit is high relative to the company's value.

pa2.evidence: The share-price fall reflects the Tarkwa lease dispute, the Windfall permit lapse and the rejected Northern Star bid, which could be fixed, but loss of Tarkwa would be permanent.

pa4.evidence: Low debt (net debt $437.4M) and a 5% dividend yield limit downside, but a gold-price collapse or lease loss could cause lasting losses.

wo1.evidence: It is a gold miner with no role in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Unit costs are rising (2026 AISC guidance $1,800-2,000/oz vs $1,645/oz in 2025), not falling with volume.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine innovation platforms; it mines gold, copper and silver.

wo4.evidence: The gold mining market cannot plausibly grow many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: Results depend directly on the gold price, currencies (rand, Australian dollar) and host-country tax and lease decisions.

ns1.evidence: As a price taker selling a commodity, it cannot pass scale savings to customers to build an advantage.

ns4.evidence: It could be larger if Windfall and acquisitions succeed, or weaker if Tarkwa is lost and mines deplete; the outcome is unclear.

va2.evidence: Gold meets real demand for savings, reserves and jewellery, but it does not solve a large, painful problem the way a new technology does.
